newsitem.title: USA: Aluminum supply deficit expected - Alumax.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum supply deficit expected - Alumax.

text.p: The aluminum market is seen moving into a supply deficit this year which will continue through to 1999, Alumax Inc chairman and chief executive, Allen Born, chairman ceo Alumax, told the Aluminum Association's annual spring meeting Wednesday.
"We see positive global economic conditions leading to supply deficits," Born said.

After a surplus over demand of 210,000 tonnes in 1996, Alumax expects a deficit in 1997 of 320,000 tonnes, which will dip to a deficit of 160,000 tonnes in 1998, but widen to a deficit of 420,000 tonnes in 1999.
The average number of days worth of demand held in inventory in 1996 was 64 days, but this is seen declining to 61 days in 1997, 54 days in 1998 and 42 days in 1999.
At year end 1996 inventory represented 54 days of demand, and this is forecast to fall to 61 days at year end 1997, 54 days in 1998 and 47 days in 1999.
Because of the decline in "inventory days", a "modest upswing bias in pricing" can be expected by 1999, Born said.
LME three month aluminum ended Wednesday trading around $1604 a tonne, up $20 a tonne. Aluminum prices have risen steadily since October 1996.
Alumax forecast world demand for primary aluminum at 21.62 million tonnes in 1997, up 5.4 pct from 1996.
In 1998 demand was seen at 22.28 million tonnes, up 3.1 pct, while in 1999 demand was seen at 23.25 million tonnes, up 4.4 pct.
World primary aluminum production in 1997 was expected to be 21.3 million tonnes, up 2.7 pct, rising 3.8 pct in 1998 to 22.12 million tonnes, and 3.2 pct in 1999 to 22.83 million tonnes.
Demand in 1996 was estimated at 20.52 million tonnes, compared with supply of 20.73 million tonnes.

Primary aluminum producing capacity in 1996 was estimated at 23.03 million tonnes, but this was seen rising to 23.43 million tonnes this year, up 1.7 pct, while capacity was seen growing 3.4 pct in 1998 to 24.23 million tonnes and 1.1 pct in 1996 to 24.49 million tonnes.
